processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Annealing produces the fully austenite (single-phase austenite) microstructure; the annealed grains are fully recovered and contain abundant annealing twins.

structures.overall_structure: fully austenite (single-phase austenite) structure with equiaxed polygonal austenite grains containing abundant straight, parallel-sided annealing twins; grains are fully recovered

phases_present.morphology: equiaxed polygonal austenite grains containing straight, parallel-sided annealing twins

characterization_methods.purpose: Observe the microstructure of the annealed fully austenite low-density steel
characterization_methods.key_findings: Abundant annealing twins are observed in the fully recovered austenite grains; the grains are equiaxed and polygonal (50 µm scale bar).

analytical_models.model_name: density–composition empirical formula for Fe–Mn–C–Al austenite steel
analytical_models.equation_role: predicts the density of Fe–Mn–C–Al austenite steel from alloying composition
analytical_models.model_note: ρ_Fe-Mn-C-Al = 8.15 − 0.101(wt%Al) − 0.41(wt%C) − 0.0085(wt%Mn) (equation 1); C addition gives the most obvious density reduction, followed by Al and Mn.

analytical_models.model_name: Al solute yield strength formula for Fe–Mn–C–Al austenite
analytical_models.equation_role: relates austenite yield strength to Al solute content

analytical_models.model_name: Mn solute yield strength formula for Fe–Mn–C–Al austenite
analytical_models.equation_role: relates austenite yield strength to Mn solute content

analytical_models.model_name: C solute yield strength formula for Fe–Mn–C–Al austenite
analytical_models.equation_role: relates austenite yield strength to C solute content

analytical_models.model_name: lattice constant–composition empirical formula for Fe–Mn–C–Al austenite
analytical_models.equation_role: relates austenite lattice constant to alloying composition
analytical_models.model_note: α_Fe-Mn-C-Al = 0.35721 + 0.0002771(wt%...) (equation 2); the equation is truncated in the source text, so the Al and Mn terms are not shown. C plays a more positive role in austenite lattice constant expansion than Al and Mn.

unmapped_findings: Fully austenite Fe–Mn–C–Al low-density steel composition: Mn 12–30 wt%, Al 5–12 wt%, C 0.6–1.2 wt%, to stabilize the austenite structure at room temperature (b0033).
To stabilize the austenite matrix of Fe–Mn–C–(Al) low-density steel and suppress ferrite formation, higher contents of Mn and C are needed to tolerate Al addition up to >10 wt% (b0011).

Class-level mechanical properties of Fe–Mn–C–Al low-density steel (not specific to this annealed sample): yield strength up to 950 MPa, tensile strength up to 1.1 GPa, and plastic ductility not less than 40% (b0010).
Density of Fe–Mn–C–Al low-density steel exhibits between 6.2 and 7.0 g cm^-3 with Al addition from 2 to 12 wt% (b0010).
Aging (not the annealing process of this sample) of the full austenite Fe–Mn–C–Al steel at 400–650 °C for 0.5–100 h leads to decomposition γ → γ′ + γ″ → γ′ + L12(SRO) → γ + κ (b0039, b0040).

With sufficient aging or slow cooling, κ and Fe(Mn)C precipitations form within austenite grains and along grain boundaries; Fe(Mn)C carbide is common in low-Al-containing steel (<7 wt% Al), while κ precipitation occurs in high-Al-containing steel (≥7 wt% Al) (b0045).
